A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RelGNN research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including material reorganized or expanded in v2.

before.justification: V1 Tables 1–3 report original RelGNN classification, regression, and recommendation results across 30 RELBENCH tasks.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and adds component ablations, additional baseline results, and a positional-encoding experiment in Appendices C–D.

M1.justification: The core atomic-route, fusion, attention, and aggregation procedure in Equations (1)–(7) is retained. Appendix D adds an implemented schema-graph relative positional encoding that modifies messages by adding a learned, scaled positional term to address self-loops.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven RELBENCH databases and 30 tasks. Appendix A retains the dataset and task descriptions. The new ablations and positional-encoding experiment reuse existing coverage, including the existing rel-stack self-loop setting.

E2.justification: V1 compares against LightGBM and heterogeneous GraphSAGE. V2 retains these comparisons and adds evaluated GAT and GIN baselines across all 30 tasks in Tables 5–7, substantially broadening the GNN comparison. GraphSAGE corresponds to the existing Hetero-GNN baseline.

E3.justification: The main temporal splits, Table 4 sample counts, metrics, prediction heads, and losses remain unchanged. New experimental configurations include a controlled GraphSAGE-style aggregation variant without attention and the supplemental positional-encoding configuration on two rel-stack classification tasks.

E4.justification: V1 contains no component ablation. V2 Appendix C adds an attention ablation across all 30 tasks to distinguish atomic-route benefits from attention benefits. Appendix D additionally tests a positional-encoding remedy for the previously discussed self-loop limitation.

E5.justification: Both versions report main results averaged over five seeds. V2 introduces no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance-testing procedures; the additional appendix results do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 5–7 add GAT, GIN, and no-attention results across all 30 tasks. Six existing RelGNN scores change: study-adverse MAE becomes 44.461 instead of 44.681, and five recommendation entries change, including rel-amazon user-item-rate MAP from 0.87 to 0.92 and rel-stack user-post-comment from 13.76 to 14.00. Appendix D also reports a 2% improvement on both rel-stack classification tasks without absolute scores.

T1.justification: V2 explicitly defines the directed schema graph and adds the Laplacian-based mathematical construction of relative positional encoding and its message update in Appendix D. The principal message-passing equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution, 30-task scope, and up-to-25% improvement claim remain. The introduction changes the claimed number of tasks with more than 4% improvement from 15 to 17, while the abstract and conclusion qualify superiority as applying to the vast majority of tasks. The counts correspond to rounded gains of at least 4%, leaving the strict threshold wording imprecise.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the mechanism explanation around repeated bridge information and underrepresented source signals. Appendix C newly attributes gains primarily to atomic routes rather than attention. Appendix D adds schema-level scalability arguments, a self-loop remedy, and compatibility discussions for advanced aggregators and temporal encodings. Existing prediction-head limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability statement and repository link in the abstract, explains how training tables provide labels and timestamps, and documents schema-level route computation and positional-encoding implementation. These add access and implementation information without establishing changes to the existing data-processing pipeline.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of HiGPT and citations covering positional encodings, GAT, GIN, advanced aggregators, and temporal encodings. The central positioning against conventional heterogeneous GNNs and alongside prediction-head improvements remains. The meta-path discussion is largely relocated from preliminaries to related work.

P1.justification: The introduction, preliminaries, structural motivation, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. The former Method section is split into topology and architecture sections, meta-path background moves to related work, and experiments gain explicit setup, results, and limitations subdivisions. Appendices C–D extend the document structure.

P2.justification: V2 restyles the structural diagrams and revises the RDL illustration. V1 Figures 4–9 are consolidated into a six-panel Figure 4, preserving their dataset coverage. Three new ablation tables add substantial comparative displays with best and second-best highlighting.

improvement.justification: V1 left the central benefit of atomic routes confounded with its use of attention. V2 substantially addresses this deficiency through the aggregation-matched ablation and GAT/GIN comparisons across 30 tasks in Tables 5–7, strengthening evidence for the main contribution. Clearer structural explanations also help. Appendix C overstates universal superiority—GIN beats RelGNN on study-adverse—and the positional-encoding result remains underspecified, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvement.
